### F1228-pmm-alloc-below-pagesets

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED F1228 | DEFECT | med | **`Pmm::alloc_below` consulted no watermark and never entered the slowpath, so a bounded DMA allocation could drain a zone past its minimum and failed rather than reclaiming.** It walked the free lists itself and took the first block that fitted the address, whatever the zone's marks said, and returned `NoMem` without waking reclaim or the out-of-memory selector. It is now three lines of policy over `alloc_gfp`: resolve the bound to zone bits, allocate normally, re-check the block against the bound. One allocation path means the bounded request takes the same per-zone gate, owes the same lowmem reserve, and enters the same reclaim/kill retry as everything else — by construction rather than by a second copy of the gate. **Call sites (unchanged, all live):** `drv-hda/src/probe.rs:35,40` and `drv-e1000/src/imp.rs:230` via `pmm::setup::alloc_contig_below`; `drv-nvme/src/queue.rs:112` and `queue/dma.rs:18,26` via `alloc_raw_frame_below` / `alloc_contig_below`. No driver changed. | F1228. `crates/kernel/mm-pmm/src/buddy/api.rs::alloc_below`; the verified direct-DMA allocation contract is convert, allocate, verify, then narrow the zone on an unaddressable result. Tests `tests::dma_bound::{a_bounded_allocation_is_held_to_the_zones_watermark, a_bounded_allocation_that_finds_nothing_reaches_the_slowpath_mark}` (`cargo test -p pmm` 263 -> 273). **Positive control:** splicing the pre-fix free-list-scan body back in turns both RED — "unmarked allocator left 0 pages, marked one left 0" — restored GREEN. | F1228 |
| FIXED F1228 | MISSING | low | **The DMA address bound was a PFN aperture, not gfp zone bits, so the DMA and DMA32 zones were never named by any requester.** The bound is now resolved to zone bits once, at the allocator boundary, by `zone::gfp_for_pfn_limit`: at or below the DMA zone's top selects `GFP_DMA`, at or below DMA32's top selects `GFP_DMA32`, above both names no zone. **Design call, and why:** the aperture becomes a zone selection rather than staying an aperture with the zone ladder bolted onto it. Every gate below `alloc_gfp` — `zone_watermark_ok`, the `lowmem_reserve` matrix, `alloc_slowpath`'s rung selection — is indexed by zone, so keeping the aperture would have required an aperture-aware second copy of all of it that could disagree with the first. The reference does not pass an address to its page allocator either; its DMA layer converts to zone bits and then verifies with `dma_coherent_ok`, narrowing the selection one zone at a time on a block that still lands outside. Ours mirrors that ladder in `zone::narrow_zone_bits` (none -> DMA32 -> DMA -> fail), bounded at three attempts. **What this gives up, and the reference gives it up too:** a bound falling in the middle of a zone can no longer be met by scanning that zone's low blocks — the request narrows to the zone below instead, and fails if nothing there can serve it. Every in-tree requester's bound is a zone top (`DMA32_LIMIT`) or above every zone, so none is affected. `GFP_DMA` and `GFP_DMA32` now have a real requester; only `GFP_MOVABLE` is still test-only, which its own OPEN row covers. | F1228. New `crates/kernel/mm-pmm/src/zone/dma.rs`, ungated and hosted-tested (6 tests in `zone/tests/dma.rs`), plus `tests::dma_bound::{a_block_outside_the_bound_is_returned_and_a_narrower_zone_tried, a_bound_no_populated_zone_can_meet_fails_rather_than_escaping_it}`. **Positive controls:** breaking the ladder's first rung turns the two ladder unit tests and the narrowing behavioural test RED; deleting the post-allocation bound re-check turns the narrowing test RED with "allocator escaped its bound: 800". Both restored GREEN. **A control that stayed GREEN, reported as a finding about the test:** `a_bound_no_populated_zone_can_meet_fails_rather_than_escaping_it` is unmoved by deleting the bound re-check, because its fixture has nothing in any zone the bound selects, so zone selection alone already refuses — it pins the selection, not the re-check. | F1228 |

### B2264-sched-atomic-false-positive

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2264 | DEFECT | high | **624 `[BUG] scheduling while atomic` reports on one live-gnome boot, with every atomicity field ZERO — the context was NOT atomic and the check said so: the count was one BELOW the level `schedule()` had just established, and the recovery for that case could not terminate.** `schedule()`'s entry does `preempt_disable` then requires the count to read exactly `PREEMPT_DISABLED`, which is the reference's own exact comparison. A count that has been decremented once more than it was incremented wraps one below zero, so the entry increment lands back at ZERO — a value with no PREEMPT, SOFTIRQ, HARDIRQ or NMI field set, which is why the report's every field read zero and nothing was held. The old recovery treated every mismatch alike: preserve the count and defer the request to "the owner that will drop it". An under-count has no such owner, so the give-back restored the same wrong value, the caller's wait loop re-drove the schedule, and the pair repeated with nothing changing — the reports are one task's wait loop, not 624 separate violations. The reference does not defer at all here: it reports and stamps the count back to the schedule-entry level, so the accounting is self-healing. `recover` now does the same for a count below the entry level (report, `preempt_count_set(PREEMPT_DISABLED)`, schedule), and keeps the deferral only for the genuinely non-switchable cases — in-interrupt and shared-IRQ-stack — which cannot livelock because they leave the count non-zero. The report line now carries `expected=` and `reason=count-under-entry-level` vs `reason=atomic-context`, so a log can no longer say "atomic" about a context whose every field is zero. | B2264. Counts on the original boot: 0 on pre-change `main`, 0 on B2262 boot 1, 624 on B2262 boot 2 (`scratch/evidence/b2262/live-gnome-x86-run2-46s-schedatomic.log`, first at 45.474s) — boots 1 and 2 ran the SAME binary, so it is not deterministic and the B2262 change is not implicated. Decisive detail in that log: all 624 carry the same `current_tid=4283`, the same `sp`, the same `caller=wait_event.rs:168` (`park_yield` inside `wait_event_uninterruptible_untils`'s loop), and **the boot logged NOTHING ELSE from 45.474s until QEMU was killed at 46.289s** — no forward progress, which is a livelock, not 624 callers. The named B2262 suspect (an allocation under the listener locks) is RULED OUT as the cause: it cannot produce an under-count, and the mechanism above needs no allocation. Fix in `sched/src/live/schedule/atomic.rs::classify`/`recover`; tests `sched::live::schedule::atomic::tests::{count_below_entry_level_is_repaired_not_deferred, repair_restores_the_entry_level_and_lets_the_switch_run, undercounted_cpu_reaches_a_schedule_instead_of_looping_forever}` — the last drives the real entry sequence from an under-counted CPU and fails if the verdict never heals the count. Positive control: restoring the two-arm `classify` turns all three RED ("refusal never healed the count: 32 rounds, still refusing"), restored GREEN. sched 1475 -> 1478 (1483 with `debug-preempt`). `xtask kernel --check` and `make feature-gate` green on x86_64 and aarch64, each log naming this worktree. | B2264 |

### B2258-iouring-cmd-uaf

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2258 | DEFECT | high | **The io_uring external-command shim dereferences `ExternalCmd` before anything guarantees the allocation is still alive, and its two guard flags are read after the deref they would have to protect.** `done()` reads `state(cmd)` and clones `s.req`/`s.file` FIRST, then claims the terminal completion with `s.done.swap(true)` and frees the box with `Box::from_raw`. If two completions can race — and the `done` flag exists precisely because the code does not trust the driver to complete once — the loser reads through `cmd` after the winner freed it. `run_task()` has the same shape from the other side: `do_in_task` hands the bare `cmd` address to `queue_work` with no reference held, so a completion that lands in the window between queueing and the worker running frees the box under the worker, and the `s.task` CAS is a double-queue guard, not a lifetime guard. Either single-completion is a stated precondition of these `unsafe extern "C"` entry points (in which case the `done`/`task` flags are dead defence and should say so) or it is not (in which case both sites are use-after-free). These are the only 2 of 440 `code/safety-missing` blocks in the tree for which no safety argument could be written, which is why they were left uncommented rather than papered over. **Resolved: `:190` was a real use-after-free, `:96` was not, and the same change settles both.** The reference's ownership rule is that the command is not a driver allocation at all: it is the ring's request, the completion hook records a result and hands the request back to the ring rather than freeing anything, and a task-work hand-off takes no reference because upstream the callback and the completion are the SAME per-request task-work node run on ONE task, so they cannot overlap. This kernel instead freed inside the completion hook and queued the hand-off on a per-CPU workqueue drained by a separate kthread, so the two CAN overlap on different CPUs -- that difference, not the flags, was the bug. So: the driver-side precondition (keep the command alive across any core hook, complete at most once, never touch it after completing) is real and is exactly what the reference requires of its own consumers, and no code at a bare-pointer boundary can enforce it -- which is why `:96` is NOT a use-after-free with respect to a second `done`, and why `claim_done` can only ever be defence against a double CQE and a double release, never a lifetime guarantee. It is still stated and ordered now: the claim happens before any field is read, because the state is only reachable through the claim's return value. `:190` was genuinely unsound: `queue_work` pushes onto a per-CPU ring woken for a worker kthread, so a completion arriving between queue and run freed the box under `run_task`, and the `task` CAS is a double-arm guard. Fixed by giving the storage a refcount, which is the nearest expressible form of the reference's 'the ring owns it': `ExternalCmd` is now an `Arc`, the pointer handed to the driver IS the driver's strong reference, the hand-off takes its own strong reference before queueing, the terminal claim consumes the driver's reference, and the ABI file object is released in `Drop` so storage and ABI object die together once the LAST reference goes. | B2256. `crates/kernel/syscalls/src/io_uring/linux_cmd.rs:96` (`done` -> `state`) and `:190` (`run_task` -> `state`); `make lint-ratchet` reports exactly these two as `crates/kernel/syscalls [code/safety-missing] 2 > 0` after the burndown. The free is `linux_cmd.rs` `drop(Box::from_raw(cmd.cast::<ExternalCmd>()))` inside `done`, after the reads at 96-100. **B2258 (fix).** Rules + tests moved to the ungated `crates/kernel/syscalls/src/io_uring_cmd_life.rs` (`+ io_uring_cmd_life/tests.rs`, 7 tests) because `io_uring.rs` carries `#![cfg(target_os = "oxide-kernel")]`, so anything written inside `linux_cmd.rs` compiles out silently. Shim call sites: `linux_cmd.rs` `done` -> `claim_terminal`, `do_in_task` -> `arm_handoff`, `run_task` -> `take_handoff`; `issue` (reached from `io_uring/iowq/run.rs:153`) hands out the driver reference with `Arc::into_raw`. Positive controls, each restored and re-confirmed GREEN after: (1) hand off without the reference (`Arc::as_ptr` instead of `Arc::clone`+`into_raw`) -> `a_completion_during_a_handoff_does_not_free_under_the_worker` RED with `storage outlives the completion while a hand-off is outstanding: left 1, right 0`, i.e. the box freed under the worker, and the whole filter aborted with SIGABRT/`unaligned tcache chunk` from the resulting double free; (2) non-atomic terminal claim (load+store) -> `racing_completions_elect_exactly_one_winner` RED with 2 winners; (3) non-atomic arm -> `racing_arms_elect_exactly_one_worker_per_callback` RED. Control (2) FIRST STAYED GREEN at 64 iterations x 8 threads -- a finding about the test, not a pass -- and only went red after adding a `Barrier` and 512 iterations; both racing tests now gate on the barrier. `cargo test -p syscalls`: 1933 passed / 6 failed, the same 6 as `main` (5 `affinity_abi` + `return_fastpath`), main being 1926/6. `xtask kernel --check` green on x86_64 and aarch64. `make lint-ratchet`: BEFORE 47 keys / 1931 findings including `crates/kernel/syscalls [code/safety-missing] 2 > 0`; AFTER 46 keys / 1929 findings with no `safety-missing` or `safety-short` key in the output at all -- the ratchet still FAILs on the 46 unrelated pre-existing keys. Baseline untouched. | B2258 |

### B2259-ioapic-pin-overflow

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2259 | DEFECT | med | **`hal-x86_64`'s vector-to-pin table could not represent its own widest pin value: the +1-biased encoding overflowed the pin field into the I/O APIC index field, and one hosted test had been red on `main` because of it.** `route_vector` packed a route as `((index + 1) << 32) | (pin as u64 + 1)`. For `pin == u32::MAX` the biased pin was `0x1_0000_0000`, which carried out of the low 32-bit field: the stored word became index 2, pin 0, so `pin_for_vector` read `encoded as u32 == 0`, its `checked_sub(1)` yielded `None`, and the route read back as absent while also naming the wrong controller. Fixed by bounds-checking at the encode boundary rather than widening or repacking the fields: the I/O APIC version register's highest-redirection-entry field is 8 bits wide, so a controller implements at most 256 entries and the widest valid pin is 255 — matching this code's own existing `& 0xff` reads of that field in `has_pin`/`gsi_pin`/`clear_at`. `route_vector` now rejects (no-ops) any `pin >= MAX_REDIR_PIN` (named constant, 256) instead of silently wrapping. | B2256 filed, B2259 fixed. `cargo test -p hal-x86_64`: 202 passed/1 failed on `main` (`bbadf81aa`) → 204 passed/0 failed after fix (added a second test for the rejection path). | FIXED B2253 | DEFECT | high | **A `security.selinux` read went to the filesystem's attribute store and never asked the label module, so the label of any object whose filesystem cannot store attributes was unreadable.** The reference answers a `security.*` read from the LSM FIRST (`fs/xattr.c: vfs_getxattr` -> `xattr_getsecurity` -> `security_inode_getsecurity` -> `selinux_inode_getsecurity`), which reads the object's IN-CORE sid and renders it; the store is reached only on the `nolsm:` fallback, i.e. only when the answer was `EOPNOTSUPP` (no module owns the name). `selinux_inode_getsecurity` never touches the filesystem, so upstream the label is readable on devtmpfs, procfs, sockfs and pipefs alike. Here `vfs_getxattr` went straight to `inode.getxattr()`, so a device node answered `EOPNOTSUPP` and an unlabelled disk file answered `ENODATA` — both of which callers read as "no label". `xattr_permission` was also wrong to be able to fail here: the reference returns 0 for the whole `security.` namespace with no DAC check (`fs/xattr.c:137-143`), and a label-module denial is `-EACCES` (`security/selinux/avc.c`), never `EPERM`. | B2253. Observed on a live-gnome boot: `pam_selinux(gdm-autologin:session): Failed to get current context for /dev/tty2: Operation not supported` (EOPNOTSUPP = -95) and `polkit.service: Failed to read SELinux context of '/usr/lib/systemd/system/polkit.service'`. Fix: `selinux_runtime::inode::xattr::{answers_getsecurity,getsecurity_value}` (pure), `fs::selinux::xattr::inode_getsecurity` (glue), called from `fs::xattr::ops::vfs_getxattr` with the `lsm_declined` (`EOPNOTSUPP`-only) fallthrough. Tests: `fs/tests/selinux_label_attribute.rs` (3, driven against the real Fedora `policy.34`) + 3 in `selinux-runtime/src/tests/inode.rs`. Positive control: disabling the hook turns 2 of the 3 RED, the storeless one with exactly `-95`. The value length is `strlen + 1` per `security/selinux/ss/services.c:1389`, so the terminator is inside the attribute. | B2253 |

### B2245-boot-wedge-gate2

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2245 | DEFECT | blocker | **Every boot that loaded an SELinux policy wedged with PID 1 spinning in `sched_yield` at 5.7 million calls a second, forever.** The status page's SEQUENCE word is a seqlock: the reference increments it once before writing the page's fields and once after, so it is EVEN whenever the page is readable and odd only inside an update, and its own comment gives the reader's contract — "If it is odd-number, kernel is updating the status, so please wait for a moment." `libselinux` waits by yielding the CPU in a loop. We published the POLICY sequence number in that word instead; it counts updates one at a time, so a single policy load left it at 1, permanently odd, and reading that page is the first thing distro userspace does after loading a policy. The seqlock is now its own counter advancing by the reference's two increments per completed update. Two further divergences the reference settled in the same read: setenforce must update the page (it carries the mode, and the reference has a dedicated notifier), and the POLICYLOAD word carries the policy sequence number (`status->policyload = seqno`), not a count of loads — a boolean commit moves that sequence, and a load counter sits still through one, so userspace would not know to flush. | B2245. Reference `security/selinux/status.c` (`status->sequence++` … `status->sequence++` around each update) and `security.h`'s `struct selinux_kernel_status` word order. Guest side, from the `libselinux.so.1` this image boots: `1e340 call sched_yield@plt; 1e345 mov 0x4(%rbx),%r12d; 1e34f test $0x1,%r12b; 1e353 jne 1e340`. Measured: PID 1 `R` with 892,133,438 syscalls at 201.5 s and 909,038,734 at 204.5 s. 6 hosted tests (`selinux::status`, `selinuxfs` page walk); positive control: one increment per update turns 4 of 6 RED, restored GREEN. The existing page test asserted the policy sequence in the seqlock word — the defect written down as the expectation — and is corrected. After: `Relabeled /dev/, /dev/shm/, /run/` 39 ms past the old freeze point, boot-smoke PASS in 46 s (`scratch/evidence/b2245/x86-selinux-seqlock-after.log`). | B2245-boot-wedge-gate2 |
| FIXED B2245 | COVERAGE | med | **A task spinning on a syscall could not be located: the non-maskable-interrupt backtrace only ever caught it in the syscall entry path, which names nothing.** Both samples of the wedged CPU resolved to `syscall_entry_work` — true of ANY task looping on a syscall, which is exactly the case worth diagnosing. The backtrace now also prints the interrupted task's USER instruction pointer and stack pointer, read from the frame the entry saved on this CPU's syscall stack. That is what pointed at `libselinux` and turned an opaque 100%-CPU freeze into a named userspace loop. | B2245. `hal_x86_64::fault::nmi_backtrace`, guarded on the interrupted frame being kernel-mode and the saved frame being user-mode. | B2245-boot-wedge-gate2 |
| FIXED B2245 | DEFECT | high | **The idle loop parked through the bare architectural halt, so a core could stop where no interrupt could reach it.** `hlt` on x86_64 and `wfi` on aarch64 do not touch the interrupt mask, and the idle path is REACHED with interrupts masked: `schedule()` runs its pick behind a saved-and-disabled mask, and the idle task resumes with whatever mask its last switch-out saved. A core that halted in that state took no timer tick, no reschedule IPI and no device interrupt for the rest of the boot; only a non-maskable interrupt could disturb it. The reference parks with `sti; hlt` — one instruction pair whose interrupt shadow makes enabling and halting inseparable — and aarch64 unmasks before `wfi` for the same reason (`wfi` completes on a pending interrupt whether or not the mask admits it, so a core parked masked wakes and then cannot service what woke it). And nothing reported it: the cross-CPU stall scan deliberately excuses a CPU that has entered the idle path, so the machine went silent with no watchdog line at all, which is exactly what the every-boot gate recorded as "a wedge with no diagnostic". `hal::CpuOps::safe_halt` is the primitive, written once per architecture; `halt` stays for the panic stop and the offline park. `sched::idle` states the contract off the target gate — the loop that uses it is kernel-target only, so a test written beside it would build nothing (`docs/53`) — and repairs plus reports a park that returns with interrupts masked, as the reference does under its own warning. After: `x86-m2-7.log` `[NMI-BT] cpu=1 rip=…8008f959 rflags=0x286` — the instruction after `sti; hlt`, interrupts admitted, heartbeat age 2-5 ms. Instruction-level check of both kernels: `sti` immediately followed by `hlt`; `msr daifclr, #0x2; dsb sy; wfi`. 6 hosted tests in `sched::idle` (1424 -> 1430). Positive controls: parking through a halt that does not admit interrupts turns 4 of 6 RED; trusting a park that returns masked turns 2 of 6 RED; restored, 6/6 GREEN. **This did not close the gate** — the remaining wedge is its own row in `known_issues.md`. | B2245-boot-wedge-gate2 |
| FIXED B2245 | COVERAGE | med | **A wedged guest could not be asked where its CPUs were, only what its tasks were.** The sysrq per-CPU dump named heartbeat age, preempt count and reschedule state, and nothing about the deferred-wake state that a task dump reports only indirectly as `W ... onwl=y`; and the smoke timeout handler typed the task, blocked-task and per-CPU keys but never the all-CPU backtrace, so no wedge investigation had ever seen a wedged CPU's instruction pointer or its interrupt mask. The dump grew `ttwu_pending` and `wake_list` columns (`sched::live::ttwu::wake_list_debug`, a bounded walk — a dump runs on a machine whose invariants are already suspect), and the handler now types the backtrace key TWICE: one sample cannot tell a spin from slow progress, and two showed the CPU advancing rather than stuck on one instruction. ### F1180-selinux-mac-policy

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |

| FIXED e67fc75b4 | DEFECT | high | **The security server was held under a SPINLOCK across the policy load, so a boot with a policy stormed `scheduling while atomic`.** The image handed to the load is CALLER memory whose pages are only demand-faulted, and the first byte of it was touched inside the closure that holds the lock — so the fault slept with preemption disabled, on every load. ### B2237-getty-restart-loop

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2237 | DEFECT | high | **A pipe reported one readiness mask for the inode instead of one per open END, so a read end whose last writer closed NEVER reported a hangup.** The reference computes the read-side bits only for a description carrying read access and the write-side bits only for one carrying write access, and the two ends say different things about a broken pipe: the read end reports HANGUP when the writer count reaches zero, the write end reports ERROR when the reader count reaches zero. Oxide's mask was direction-blind and had them crossed — it raised HUP on `readers == 0` (the WRITE end's condition) and could not raise it on `writers == 0` at all. A consumer that polls a pipe read end for nothing but `POLLHUP` — which is how "wait until the writer goes away" is written, since `POLLHUP` cannot be asked for in `events` and is only ever reported — therefore waited out its whole timeout every time. That is exactly what `Type=idle` service startup does, and it is why `serial-getty@ttyS0` took 5.000 s per attempt and never reached its `ExecStart` at all. | B2237. `fs::pipe::pollmask::pipe_poll_mask` — 11 hosted tests covering both ends, both directions, empty/full, and the crossed-condition cases. Positive control: restoring the old direction-blind body turns 10 of the 11 RED (`a_read_end_whose_last_writer_closed_reports_a_hangup` among them); restored, 11/11 GREEN. `cargo test -p fs` 1961 passed, 0 failed. Consumer measured in the guest: a byte-for-byte clone of the generated unit loops at 5.006 s with `Type=idle` (`Started` 29.887 → `Deactivated successfully` 34.892 → restart counter climbing) and does not loop at all with `Type=simple` (started 57.952, still running at the 13 s stop) — same binary, same fds, same tty; the only difference is the idle-pipe wait. | B2237-getty-restart-loop |
| FIXED B2237 | DEFECT | med | `serial-getty@ttyS0.service` exits SUCCESSFULLY after exactly 5.000 s and restart-loops — 23 restarts in one 129 s boot, at a metronomic 5.4 s period. **The exit status was honest and the process was never there: agetty is not executed at all.** `ExecStart` carries systemd's `-` prefix, and the unit is `Type=idle`, so the child waits on the manager's idle pipe for `POLLHUP` before `exec`. With the pipe hangup unreportable (row above) that wait always ran its 5 s course. Straced under a clone of the unit, the `strace -ff -o` output files were never created — nothing ever ran. agetty itself is fine on this kernel: run by hand on `/dev/ttyS0`, both with the device name and with `-` on an `O_RDWR` fd, it reaches `oxide login:` and blocks in `read` for the full 10 s bound (killed by the harness, exit 137), and the same run on `/dev/tty2` prints `/etc/issue` and waits. | B2233 boot `x86_64-185055`: `Started` / `Deactivated successfully` pairs at 91.4→96.4, 96.8→101.8, 102.1→107.1, …, restart counter reaching 23. B2237 in-guest probes: cloned unit reproduces at 5.006 s; `ls -l /tmp/agS.*` → `No such file or directory` after three restarts; manual runs exit 137 after the full bound. | B2237-getty-restart-loop |

### F863-oom-allocation-context-entry

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED F863 | MISSING | high | **No allocation-context out-of-memory entry: only the user-fault fill leg selected a victim, so a kernel allocation that could not be satisfied returned failure with nothing killed and no memory recovered.** `Buddy::alloc` returned `Error::NoMem` straight out of `alloc_inner`; `sched::oom::out_of_memory` had exactly two callers repo-wide, the fault leg and the cgroup limit path. The frame allocator now has the reference's slowpath: on exhaustion it enters a reclaim/retry loop and, once reclaim has stopped making progress, selects and kills a victim, then re-attempts the allocation rather than failing it. Selection is not duplicated — the existing `sched::oom` entry point is called. Context gate: an atomic caller fails immediately (it cannot sleep, so it can neither reclaim nor wait for a victim), which is the reference's `!can_direct_reclaim -> nopage` edge; we have no GFP flags, so that is the whole gate. An order above `PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER` reclaims and retries but never kills, because a kill frees pages and not contiguity. A single-holder guard serialises selection across CPUs and against re-entry from the allocations the kill path itself makes; a caller that cannot take it retries rather than queueing, as the reference's `mutex_trylock(&oom_lock)` does. `kswapd::direct_reclaim_once` now reports whether it freed a page, which is the progress signal the retry counter reads. Residue filed as its own row: the number of selector invocations per allocation is bounded, standing in for the absent reaper. | F863. Decision machine in the ungated `mm-pmm/src/oom_entry.rs` (`slowpath_allowed`, `may_invoke_oom`, `next_step`, `after_oom`, `run_slowpath`), driven by injected reclaim/alloc/kill actions so the whole loop runs hosted; `buddy/api.rs::alloc_slowpath` supplies the three real actions. `cargo test -p pmm` 192 -> 202, 0 failed. Positive controls, each RED then restored GREEN at 202/0: reinstating the defect (`next_step` never answering `InvokeOom`, exactly as the old allocator behaved) fails 4 — `allocation_succeeds_on_the_memory_a_victim_released`, `nothing_killable_fails_the_allocation_at_once`, `contended_selector_retries_and_stays_bounded`, `kill_invocations_are_bounded_per_allocation`; killing on first failure instead of reclaiming first fails 2 — `reclaim_precedes_any_kill`, `progressing_reclaim_never_reaches_the_killer`. ### B2057-uniprocessor-spinlock-wedge

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2057 | DEFECT | high | **A uniprocessor x86_64 boot wedged in early userspace because a spinning lock's owner could be descheduled inside its critical section.** Root cause, in two halves. (1) `Spinlock`/`RwLock` disabled NOTHING on acquire, where the reference makes `spin_lock` = `preempt_disable()` + acquire (and on a uniprocessor build the preempt-disable IS the lock) — so any voluntary reschedule reached from inside a section handed the CPU away with the lock still held, and with one CPU nothing could run the owner again. (2) THE owner that did so: `file->f_pos_lock` was a `Spinlock`, held across `submit_readahead` + `dispatch_read`, i.e. across ext4 -> virtio-blk -> `park_blk_checked` -> `schedule()`. In the reference that field is a `struct mutex` taken by `__fdget_pos`, precisely because the region it covers waits for the device. Every buffered `read(2)`/`readv(2)`/`write(2)` on a regular file took it, which is why the wedge always landed during rootfs I/O and always looked like a different lock. Fix: the gate (Linux ordering exactly — acquire = disable-then-spin, `spin_unlock_irqrestore` = release, restore flags, enable, `spin_trylock` = disable then enable on failure, `spin_lock_bh` unchanged because `local_bh_disable` already raises the count); `f_pos_lock` becomes a sleeping lock over the crate's one sleepable primitive; and new tasks start at `FORK_PREEMPT_COUNT` (2) because a switching task now carries both `schedule()`'s disable and the forgotten rq lock, the invariant `finish_task_switch` asserts. Folds the older duplicate row that described the same wedge from fewer samples. | B2057. Measured on the boot gate: `-smp 1` x86 was **2/5** before and is **5/5** after (5 sequential runs, all attempt 1, 64-77 s); `-smp 1` aarch64 1/1; `make smoke` (SMP) green both arches. Hosted causality, RED before / GREEN after (positive control run both ways): `sched::preempt::hosted_tests::{a_reschedule_cannot_be_taken_while_a_spinlock_is_held, irqsave_and_rwlock_sections_are_equally_unpreemptible, nested_spinlock_sections_stay_unpreemptible_until_the_outermost_release, a_never_run_task_starts_owing_exactly_what_the_switch_tail_pays_back}`, `sync::preempt_gate::tests` (4), `vfs::file::pos_lock::tests` (2). The owner was NAMED, not guessed: with the gate in place the pre-existing violation announced itself as `[BUG] scheduling while atomic: preempt_count=2 ... caller=drv-virtio-blk/src/modern/state.rs:140` on the first boot. | B2057 |

### B2050-tcp-half-open-ack-number

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2050 | DEFECT | med | **A completing acknowledgement for a half-open TCP request was accepted regardless of its acknowledgement NUMBER.** `deliver_tcp_to_request` never inspected `hdr.ack`, so with `TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT` off any ACK-bearing segment fell through into the connection state machine, whose SYN-RECV arm called `advance_snd_una(hdr.ack)` and established unconditionally: an off-path segment that guessed the 4-tuple and the receive window finished a handshake without ever guessing the sequence this side chose for its own SYN-ACK. Re-verified against the reference before implementing, and the recorded shape of the fix was WRONG in two ways worth recording: the reference does not drop silently, it answers with one reset built at the sequence the segment claimed to acknowledge; and it decides at the REQUEST, before the child exists, with a strict `ack == snt_isn + 1` equality rather than a window. The full-socket SYN-RECEIVED arm is a different rule -- `!before(ack, snd_una) && !after(ack, snd_nxt)`, one reset and no challenge acknowledgement -- and both are now implemented, in the reference's order: plain SYN repeat, then the acknowledgement number, then the receive window, then the reset and SYN bits, then completion. Judging the acknowledgement before the reset bit closes a second hole the row did not name: a blind `RST\|ACK` that guessed the window used to tear down a half-open, and now cannot. | B2050. Decision in the ungated `net::tcp_conn::synrecv` (`request_segment`, `socket_ack_acceptable`, `in_window`, `end_seq`); the two act-on sites are `stack::tcp_reqsk::deliver_tcp_to_request` and the SYN-RECV arm of `tcp_conn::io::input_with_header`. `cargo test -p net` 2484 -> 2509: 18 in `tcp_conn::synrecv::tests`, 3 in `tcp_conn::io::synrecv_socket_tests`, 4 in `stack::tcp_req_tests` over real segments on the delivery path. Positive controls, each RED then restored GREEN: reinstating the defect in `request_segment` (the acknowledgement check removed exactly as the old code had it) fails 8 -- 5 decision cases and 3 delivery-path cases, including the blind-reset one; disabling the full-socket gate in `io.rs` fails both socket cases. `make feature-gate-x86` and `feature-gate-arm` both clean. | Chris Watkins |

| FIXED F852 | MISSING | low | **`ZCRX_REG_IMPORT` and `ZCRX_CTRL_EXPORT` reported `ENXIO`/`EOPNOTSUPP`.** Both are implemented. Exporting hands out a descriptor that names one instance; adopting resolves that descriptor, takes its own table slot and its own instance id, and states nothing else — an adoption naming a receive queue, a refill depth, an area, a region or a notification descriptor is `EINVAL`, and a descriptor that carries no instance is `EBADF`. The lifetime is TWO counts, not one: the owning handle keeps the instance allocated, while a separate user count decides when the device queue is closed and the caller's buffers reclaimed. The exported descriptor is itself a user, so an adopted instance survives its exporter going away, and an instance every ring has let go cannot be adopted back into service. | FIXED PENDING | MISSING | blocker | **x86 boots multiboot2 (BIOS/CSM) only — no UEFI path, so the kernel cannot be loaded on a board without a CSM.** The premise was wrong in both halves. `grub2-mkrescue` was already writing a HYBRID ISO carrying two El Torito boot images — a BIOS one and a UEFI one — and GRUB's x86_64-efi build loads the same kernel through the same multiboot2 entry-address tag after exiting boot services, so the kernel's handoff needed no change at all. What was genuinely absent was any way to SELECT UEFI firmware in the harness, any gate that would fail if the UEFI path broke, and correct text in the boot specs, all three of which this branch adds. The kernel's own multiboot2 header carries no boot-services tag and no EGA console tag, which is what makes the firmware-agnostic handoff work. | Boot evidence: `OXIDE_QEMU_UEFI=1 tools/boot-smoke.sh x86` reached live userspace in 87 s on the first attempt, serial RX probe answered. ISO evidence: the El Torito catalog reports `img 1 BIOS /boot/grub/i386-pc/eltorito.img` AND `img 2 UEFI /efi.img`. **Positive control:** an otherwise identical ISO rebuilt BIOS-only (`grub2-mkrescue -d /usr/lib/grub/i386-pc`, catalog then reports only the BIOS image) boots under the same OVMF firmware to `BdsDxe: No bootable option or device was found` with ZERO kernel output lines and zero entry-trampoline markers — so the passing gate is measuring the UEFI path and not a silent BIOS fallback. New gate: `make smoke-uefi-x86`. | B1984 |
| FIXED PENDING | MISSING | med | **No FADT parse — no ACPI reset.** Half of this row (the reset half) is closed here; the poweroff half stays open with a corrected reason in `known_issues.md`. The FADT is now decoded and the reset register it describes is honoured. `reboot(2)` on x86 walks a real ladder in the reference's order — the firmware-described reset register, then the legacy keyboard controller's reset pulse, then the chipset reset-control port, then a triple fault as the terminal rung — instead of jumping straight to the triple fault. The reset register is admitted through the reference's ladder: table revision 2 or later, the flag bit that claims it, and an address space of port, memory or bus-0 PCI config. The declared bit width and offset are deliberately ignored, matching the reference, because firmware fills them wrongly often enough that honouring them would refuse resets the hardware performs. | `firmware::acpi::fadt` (new): `parse_fadt` + `reset_action`, both ungated and hosted-tested — 15 new tests. `power::reset` (new): ladder order and port encodings, ungated, 6 new tests; `power::reset::x86` performs the writes. Offsets are pinned by reproducing all five conformant FADT lengths from the field offsets themselves, so a whole-struct drift goes red, not just a single field. **Positive controls (12, each reinstated then restored):** shifting the flags offset by one, shifting the sleep-control offset, removing the revision gate, removing the flag-bit gate, removing the PCI device/function bound, retyping a legacy PM block out of port space, dropping the 64-bit DSDT pointer precedence, moving the triple fault off the end of the ladder, adding the firmware rung when no register exists, duplicating a rung, and dropping the reset-control read-modify-write mask — all went RED; all restored GREEN. | B1984 |

Iterator targets exist for programs, maps and links; their stubs are published in the same object the LSM hooks are, so one attach-target mechanism serves both. `BPF_LINK_CREATE` with the iterator attach type mints an iterator link in the one link id registry, and `BPF_ITER_CREATE` mints a descriptor whose read walks the target in id order, running the program per object and once at the end. Verifier controls pin the two-slot read-only context and the two-valued step answer, each against the nearest shape that must be refused. | NEXT |

| FIXED 833887264 | low | Landlock erratum 3 was not advertised because the ledger said refer checks omitted the mount-point hierarchy after reaching a directory disconnected from a bind root. | Re-audit found the implementation already carries the reference's two-stage mask walk: `collect_domain_accesses` consumes the disconnected ancestry, then `walk::from` resumes at the saved mount root and crosses its attachment hierarchy. Now follows the frame's entry tag: on a `syscall` frame `rax` is the recorded stop value and `orig_rax` the syscall number; on a trap frame `rax` is the architectural register and `orig_rax` is the no-syscall marker, which is what the core-dump block already reported for the same frame. | `x86_trap_frame_reports_no_syscall_and_the_architectural_rax`, `x86_setregs_on_a_trap_frame_installs_the_architectural_rax`. | B1706 |

| FIXED B1720 | high | `fsmount(2)` returns an anon-inode fd over a deferred mount object, not an `O_PATH` fd over a real vfsmount in an anonymous mount namespace. The fd carries `mnt_id == 0`, is `FileType::Regular` so it is `ENOTDIR` as a dirfd, is invisible to `statmount`/`listmount`, and between `fsmount` and `move_mount` the mount exists nowhere and can be neither observed nor referenced. `FSMOUNT_NAMESPACE` is unimplementable until that changes. Also missing: the `SB_NOUSER → EINVAL` check after mount creation, and `FMODE_NEED_UNMOUNT`/dissolve-on-close semantics. | `fsmount_common/fd.rs` `install_fd` → `vfs/src/file/model.rs` `File::new` (`mnt_id = 0`); `pathresolve/at.rs` rejects a non-directory dirfd. `move_mount` mode (a) grafts the superblock through a private-inode side channel instead. Blocks `432`. **Fixed by B1720:** `fsmount` now creates a REAL mount in an anonymous mount namespace (`create_anon_mount`) and returns an `O_PATH` fd over it, so the fd carries a real `mnt_id`, resolves as a dirfd, and dissolves its mount on close if never moved (`File`'s teardown → `dissolve_anon`, Linux's `__fput` → `dissolve_on_fput`). `move_mount` grafts that same mount, so the id is stable across the move. NOTE on the row's own text: invisibility to `statmount`/`listmount` was NOT a defect — `grab_requested_mnt_ns` selects the caller's namespace, so an anonymous mount is correctly invisible there. 9 hosted tests; positive control turns 3 red. | B1720 |
| FIXED B1719 | high | **`hidepid=` / `subset=pid` are NOT a parameter-table problem — procfs cannot express them at all.** Of the 22 registered filesystem types only 5 (`tmpfs`, `ramfs`, `ext4`, `autofs`, `fuse`) even receive the mount data string; the other 17, `proc` included, take `_` and discard it. And `procfs::static_files::proc_root()` returns a **process-global cached `Arc`**, so every `mount -t proc` in every namespace shares ONE root inode, leaving nowhere for per-mount option state. Per-mount `hidepid=` needs per-superblock root inodes first. **Consequence for the security framing: listing `hidepid` in a parameter table would NOT make `ProtectProc=` work — only implementing it does. Conversely a table that OMITS `hidepid` makes the support probe answer "no", and systemd then correctly stops claiming a confinement it is not getting.** Omission is the cheap honest fix; implementation is the real one. | `crates/kernel/syscalls/src/fsmount_common/registry.rs:118` (proc ctor discards data); `crates/kernel/procfs/src/static_files.rs:73-76` (cached singleton root). **Fixed by B1719:** the singleton is gone — `ProcfsFs::new(info)` builds a root inode per mount carrying that mount's `Arc<ProcFsInfo>`, published in `sb.s_fs_info` as the reference does. `hidepid=`/`subset=`/`gid=` are declared and enforced: `subset=pid` clears lookup and readdir of non-process entries, `hidepid` gates pid dirs at NO_ACCESS on lookup and INVISIBLE on readdir through `has_pid_permissions`. The reference follows the trailing component inside the SAME walk (`open_last_lookups` resolves the leaf, `step_into(WALK_TRAILING)` picks the link up and the walk continues on its target). ### B1719-procfs-per-superblock-root

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B1719 | DEFECT | high | **`procfs::static_files::proc_root()` was a process-global cached `Arc`, so every `mount -t proc` in every namespace shared ONE root inode.** There was nowhere for a mount's own options to live, which is why `hidepid=`/`subset=` could not be expressed at all and `ProtectProc=`/`ProcSubset=` silently did nothing for every service that asked for them. The reference builds a fresh root inode per superblock in `proc_fill_super` and shares only the static `proc_dir_entry` skeleton (which `crate::reg` already is). Now: `ProcfsFs::new(info)` builds its own root per mount, the root carries `Arc<ProcFsInfo>`, and the same `Arc` is published in `sb.s_fs_info` where the reference keeps it. | `crates/kernel/procfs/src/fs_info.rs` (identity + decisions, ungated), `fs_impl.rs`, `static_files.rs::build_root`, `live/root.rs`. Guest proof on both arches, one `subset=pid` mount: x86 `sub_meminfo=0 sub_pids=59`, arm `sub_meminfo=0`, zero faults — against `sub_meminfo=1` before. | B1719 |
| FIXED B1719 | MISSING | high | **`hidepid=` and `subset=` were undeclared and unimplemented**; the parameter table was `Some(&[])`, so `mount -t proc -o hidepid=2` returned EINVAL — honest, but the confinement was simply absent. Both are now declared and ENFORCED: `subset=pid` removes every non-process entry from lookup and readdir (Linux `proc_lookup`/`proc_readdir` `pidonly` gate), and `hidepid` gates pid directories at the reference's two thresholds — `HIDEPID_NO_ACCESS` on lookup, `HIDEPID_INVISIBLE` on readdir — through the same `has_pid_permissions` ladder, including the `gid=` group exemption and the absolute `ptraceable` mode. | `procfs::fs_info` 16 hosted tests incl. every accepted spelling, the rejected values (`3`, `5`, `OFF`, `0x2`), the threshold split (noaccess lists but does not open), the group exemption, and that `ptraceable` ignores it. Enforcement sites: `live/root.rs` (lookup + readdir), `live/pid_access.rs::pid_visible`. | B1719 |
| FIXED B1719 | DEFECT | med | **A filesystem constructor's parameter slice is NOT its option source, and reading it silently dropped every option.** `mount(2)` carries options in the DATA BLOB; the slice holds only values that are pinned open files (`FSCONFIG_SET_FD`). The first cut of this lane read the slice, so every hosted test passed while the guest showed `meminfo` inside a `subset=pid` mount. The wiring decision now lives in `fs_info::info_for_mount(data, pinned)` — ungated, so it is testable — and `vfs::fs::split_monolithic` is the ONE splitter, extracted from `generic_parse_monolithic` rather than copied. | `a_mounts_options_come_from_the_blob_and_never_from_the_pinned_slice` fails against the shape that shipped. | FIXED 4905b1ebd | DEFECT | high | **A `#DF` (double fault) — kernel stack overflow — under a burst of serial-driven work.** Typing one compound command at the debug shell (`mkdir`; two `mount -t proc`; three `ls \| grep -c`; one deliberately-failing `mount -o hidepid=3`) double-faults the guest at t=7.73s: `vec=8 (#DF) rip=ffffffff8006d7af rsp=fffffb0000006000 rbx=00000000000003f8`. `rbx` is the COM1 base and `rsp` is on a stack guard page, so this is the guard-page catch of a stack overflow in the serial/klog path, not a procfs fault. NOT caused by this lane: the same kernel runs a plain `mount -t proc` + `ls` probe clean, and so does `origin/main`. What is not yet known is the depth chain that overflows — the fault is 12 frames of `[FAULT]` register dump with no backtrace. | Reproduced once on `B1719` x86 with the compound probe; `origin/main` and `B1719` both clean with the single-mount probe (`plain_meminfo=1`, 0 faults, exit=0 on both). Log kept: the `[FAULT]` block at `[7.730]`. Needs a lane with `debug-stack-guard` to name the overflowing path. | unowned |

### B1720-fsmount-real-vfsmount

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B1720 | DEFECT | high | **`fsmount(2)` returned an anon-inode fd over a deferred object, not a mount.** The fd carried `(sb, root)` and nothing else: `mnt_id == 0`, `FileType::Regular` (so `ENOTDIR` as a dirfd), no mount object at all between `fsmount` and `move_mount`, and nothing to tear down if the fd was simply closed. The reference creates a real `vfsmount`, parks it in an ANONYMOUS mount namespace, and hands back an `O_PATH` fd with `FMODE_NEED_UNMOUNT`. Implemented: `vfs::mount::create_anon_mount` builds a real mount (own id, own root) in a namespace flagged `is_anon`, `fsmount` installs a path fd over it, and `File`'s teardown dissolves it if it was never moved — Linux's `__fput` → `dissolve_on_fput`, at the same place. `move_mount(2)` now grafts THAT mount (`graft_anon_mount_at`), so the id is stable across the move instead of being minted at graft time. | `crates/kernel/vfs/src/mount/anon.rs`, `mntns.rs` (`is_anon`, `allocate_anon`), `file/lifetime.rs` (dissolve hook), `432_fsmount.rs`, `429_move_mount.rs`. 9 hosted tests in `vfs/tests/mount_anon_ns.rs`; positive control: making the namespace non-anonymous turns 3 of them RED. `make smoke` PASS both arches (arm 60s, x86 101s, attempt 1). | B1720 |
| FIXED B1720 | DEFECT | med | **An anonymous mount was reaped the instant it was created.** `Mount` keys its namespace by id only, with no reference — fine for a mount in a task's namespace, fatal for one whose namespace nothing else holds: `MntNamespace::drop` runs `reap_ns`, which unpublished the mount that had just been published. Linux's `mount` points at its `mnt_ns` with a reference; ours now holds one for the anonymous case (`Mount::anon_ns`), released on graft or dissolve. | Found by the first run of `an_fsmounted_filesystem_is_a_real_mount_before_it_is_moved_anywhere`: `mount_by_id` returned `None` immediately after a successful publish. | B1720 |

### B1723-serial-stack-overflow-df

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED 4905b1ebd | DEFECT | high | **CORRECTED by B1724 — the earlier prescription in this row was wrong and must not be acted on.** There IS a per-CPU hardirq stack (`hal_x86_64::init_percpu_hardirq_stack`, `gs:[24]`), the IRQ entry asm (`oxide_irq_common`) DOES switch RSP to it, and it is armed before the first `sti` on the BSP (`kmain/early.rs:347`, IRQs still masked) and on every AP (`smp_x86.rs:205`, explicitly before its `sti`). Arming verified at both call sites. | unowned |

### B1736-getlink-single-device

### B1737-carrier-model

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |

| FIXED B1737 | DEFECT | blocker | **The kernel installed the emulator's guest address on every virtio-net link at boot, so the network manager never owned the device and never ran DHCP.** `pci-boot` set `10.0.2.15/24` plus a default route on each registered interface, calling it "the boot-time v1 network identity". A kernel does not know its own IPv4 identity — a DHCP client learns it — and a manager that finds a link already carrying an address and a default route it did not configure marks the device externally-connected and declines to own it. It then never activates the link, never performs DHCP, and never publishes the DNS servers the lease carries, which is why `/etc/resolv.conf` had no `nameserver` line and names failed while a query aimed at a server's address still worked. | Guest before: `eth0:connected (externally)`, address present but no `nameserver`. After: `eth0:connected`, `inet 10.0.2.15/24 … dynamic … valid_lft 86345sec` — the `dynamic` flag and the lease lifetime are the proof it came from the DHCP server rather than the seed. | B1737 |
| FIXED B1737 | DEFECT | blocker | **Carrier lived in the same flags word userspace writes, so bringing a link up cleared it.** The reference keeps carrier out of `dev->flags` entirely — it is `__LINK_STATE_NOCARRIER` in `dev->state`, owned by the driver through `netif_carrier_on`/`off` — and derives `IFF_RUNNING` / `IFF_LOWER_UP` at read time in `dev_get_flags`, while `__dev_change_flags` never takes the volatile bits from a caller. Here carrier was a stored `IFF_RUNNING` bit in the writable word, so an ordinary "bring this link up" cleared it and the link reported no carrier the instant anyone administered it. The manager, having just brought the device up itself, was told there was no carrier and refused: `Connection 'eth0' is not available on device eth0 because device has no carrier`. Now `IfaceEntry::carrier` is a separate driver-owned bit, `iff::dev_get_flags` derives the two reported bits from it, and `IFF_VOLATILE` is masked out of every userspace write. | Guest: `<NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP>` → `<BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP>`, and `WIRED-PROPERTIES.CARRIER: off` → the device reaching `connected`. Hosted: five tests covering derivation while down/up/with/without carrier, that a caller cannot forge the bits, and that the volatile mask keeps every administrative bit writable. | B1737 |
| FIXED B1737 | DEFECT | high | **Two ways to read interface flags, and the link dump used the raw one.** `snapshot_in_ns` reported flags while `iface_flags` returned the stored word, and the `RTM_GETLINK` builder discarded the snapshot's value and re-read the raw one — so the derived carrier bits never reached the wire and a device with carrier still reported `NO-CARRIER`. `iface_flags` is now the single accessor and derives, as the reference funnels every reader through `dev_get_flags`. | `rtnetlink/iface.rs` took `stack.ifaces.iface_flags(id)` and dropped `snap.flags`. | B1737 |

The pre-install invocation is deleted; the one post-install invocation remains the only cgroup self-test owner. | `cargo test -p kmain --lib --features debug-cgroup --no-fail-fast` and `cargo check -p kmain --features debug-cgroup` pass; source has exactly one `cgroup::selftest::run()`, after `sched::cgroup::install()`. | B1889-cgroup-selftest-order |
| FIXED 0eafc98ba | DEFECT | high | **`make qemu-x86-debug` fails every time: PID 1 gets ESRCH writing its own pid into its own cgroup, and the service manager freezes.** At guest t≈28.5 s, `write("1")` to `/init.scope/cgroup.procs` returns `-3`, and the manager prints `Failed to create /init.scope control group: No such process` then `Freezing execution.` — so the boot never reaches a login and the target appears to hang. The cause is `sched::cgroup::migrate_hook` resolving the writer through a registry scan (`resolve_user_pid` / `lookup_by_vpid`) that misses for the caller's own vpid, instead of simply using the calling task the way the `vpid == 0` path already does. The reference never returns ESRCH for a process writing its own pid into a cgroup it just created. It reproduces only under `debug-all` because `debug-syscall`'s per-syscall trace widens the window; the defect is not the tracing. Compilation is clean — this is not the feature-gated-compile-error class. | Full boot capture with `--features debug-all`: the ESRCH write, both manager errors, and the freeze. `crates/kernel/sched/src/cgroup.rs` ~156-178. | unowned |

### B1739-cgroup-exit-side-table

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B1739 | DEFECT | high | **A task's exit state was recorded in a map keyed by tid, beside the task, where it could disagree with the task itself.** `CGROUP_EXITS: BTreeMap<u32, Weak<Task>>` was consulted by `migrate_hook` to refuse a migration for a task on its way out. The reference has no such table: `cgroup_procs_write_start` tests `PF_EXITING` ON THE TASK. Two records of one fact can disagree, and this one did — an instrumented boot caught the gate refusing PID 1, a task that is plainly neither reaped nor a zombie, so its tid was in the table while it was alive. Replaced with `Task::exiting`, set at the head of both exit paths exactly where the table was written, so the flag is per-Task-object and a recycled tid cannot inherit a stale answer. | Instrumented boot: `[cgprobe] exit-gate ESRCH vpid=1` while `resolve` succeeded, so the refusal came from the table and not from the lookup. Hosted: `the_exiting_flag_lives_on_the_task_and_starts_clear`. The table, its `Weak` values, and the four imports that existed only for it are gone; `cargo build -p sched` is warning-clean. | B1739 |
| FIXED 0eafc98ba | DEFECT | high | **`make qemu-x86-debug` still fails: PID 1 is still refused its own cgroup, and the cause is NOT the side table.** With the table removed the failure is unchanged — `Failed to create /init.scope control group: No such process` at t≈28.5 s, then `Freezing execution.`, verified on a live `--features debug-all` boot of this branch (log confirmed to be the new kernel: the probe strings are absent). So the ESRCH now comes from one of the other two exits in `migrate_hook`: the vpid resolve returning nothing, or returning a task that is genuinely reaped/zombie, or `cgroup::migrate_process` itself refusing. Note `lookup_by_vpid` falls back to "any group member if the leader has already exited" — a fallback that can hand back a DEAD thread, which the exit gate would then correctly refuse; that is the first thing to check. The earlier instrumented run measured the OLD code and named the table, so it does not narrow the remaining paths. | Live `debug-all` boot on this branch, t=28.5 s, both manager errors present. | unowned |

### B1740-cgroup-skip-exiting

| FIXED B1740 | DEFECT | blocker | **`make qemu-x86-debug` froze at boot because `migrate_hook` reported ESRCH for a task on its way out.** The reference does not: `cgroup_migrate_add_task` returns without acting when `PF_EXITING` is set — *"@task either already exited or can't exit until the end"* — and the part that CAN fail, `cgroup_procs_write_start`, rejects only a pid that resolves to nothing (ESRCH) or a kthread pinned by `PF_NO_SETAFFINITY` (EINVAL). ### C269-stack-gates-in-routine-path

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |

| FIXED C269 | COVERAGE | high | **`frame-gate` and `stack-gate` existed but ran nowhere, so both sat RED on `main` for a month while every routine gate stayed green.** They were reachable only by typing the Makefile target by hand: `make ci` ran `lint-ratchet audit-counts matrix-gate hosted-gate test-build-gate test build build-debug`, and `.githooks/pre-push` ran `lint-ratchet`, `hosted-gate`, `test-build-gate`, `feature-gate` and (main only) `boot-smoke` — neither included them. The only other home was `.github/workflows/pr.yml`, which has taken no automatic trigger since 2026-07-04, so the gates have never executed in CI either. What got through: an 8192 B lock array inlined into per-namespace state (B1727), giving a function reachable from softirq receive a 9256 B frame and leaving the worst interrupt-reachable path 2.5 KiB from the guard page — the intermittent serial `#DF`. A per-function ceiling structurally cannot catch a chain that sums, and a type-check cannot see a frame at all; only these two, read off a linked ELF, can. Both are now in `make ci` and in the pre-push hook for any push touching kernel/driver/arch surfaces, bypassable with `SKIP_STACK_GATE=1`. Wired now specifically because B1727 and B1728 took both gates green on both arches for the first time, so they cannot start red and be ignored again. | `make -j2 frame-gate stack-gate` on this branch: 4/4 PASS, rc=0. Positive control — `make -j2 stack-gate STACK_DEPTH_CEILING=5000` exits **2** with `make: *** [Makefile:291: stack-gate-x86] Error 1`, so a failure propagates through the new wiring rather than being swallowed. `bash -n .githooks/pre-push` clean. | C269 |

### C270-irq-stack-depth-domain

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED C270 | COVERAGE | high | **The interrupt path was invisible to the stack-depth gate, which is why the `#DF` was found by dying rather than by a check.** The walker follows direct call edges only, and every hardware interrupt handler in this kernel is reached through a registered function pointer — the MSI vector table, the x86 line-handler table, the nine softirq slots, the NAPI poll list, the tick-poll hook and the exit-to-user hook. So the receive path measured **8 bytes** deep and `drv_serial::deliver` 32, and the gate's own docstring recorded the gap rather than closing it ("INTERRUPTS AND EXCEPTION ENTRY are not modelled"). The target sets are finite and enumerable — each table has a handful of registration sites, all in this tree — so they are now named in `tools/irq-edges-<arch>.tsv` and merged into the call graph before the walk. With 23 edges resolved on x86_64 the interrupt path reports its real depth for the first time: **8704 B of the 16384 B interrupt stack**. | `make irq-gate-x86` PASS at a 12000 B ceiling, printing 8704 (`oxide_irq_exit_to_user`) and 8432 (`oxide_irq_dispatch`). Positive control: `--irq-fail 8000` exits **1** naming both roots. Without the map the same roots report 7600/7872, and `rx_isr_msi` reports 8. | C270 |
| FIXED C270 | COVERAGE | high | **The hardirq stack had no budget of its own.** It is a different 16384 B from the task stack with a different worst case: the entry asm deliberately does not re-switch when an interrupt arrives while already on it, and the softirq drain runs with interrupts unmasked, so a second entry lands on top of whatever the drain has already spent. A single ceiling shared with task stacks cannot express that. `--irq-roots` / `--irq-fail` add a second domain rooted at the two functions the entry asm calls after switching SP, with a 12000 B ceiling — the 4 KiB below the stack size is not slack, it is the nested interrupt's stack. | New `irq-gate` target, in `make ci` and in the pre-push hook alongside `frame-gate`/`stack-gate`. | C270 |
| FIXED C270 | COVERAGE | med | **The gate's pass/fail decision had no test.** `--self-test` covered the accounting — prologue summation, the arch return-address difference, recursion, indirect flagging, the blocking tail, allowlist identity — and stopped short of the layer that turns a number into an exit code, which is the layer that actually merges or blocks a defect. Extracted as `verdict()` and tested with a positive control per branch, each asserting the intended verdict fires AND the others stay empty so a rule that fires on everything cannot pass. The case that matters: a path one byte deeper than its recorded budget must be `worse`; a ratchet written `>=` instead of `>` lets a path grow without limit one byte at a time with every run green. | Positive control run: relaxing that comparison makes `--self-test` fail with `AssertionError: []`; restoring it passes. | C270 |

### B1979-gnome-segfault-regression-triage

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED (this branch) | DEFECT | High | The file-mapping fill gave up on the FIRST read that made no progress and turned it into a fatal fault, which reaches userspace as a killing signal. The reference has no short-read concept at that point: a page is uptodate or it is not, it re-reads a not-uptodate page ONCE synchronously, and only a read that actually ERRORS becomes a fault. Two conditions were therefore lethal here and are not in the reference — a transient no-progress read (page-cache build race, extent boundary) that the next read satisfies, and a file that SHRANK while the fault was in flight, whose extent was still being judged against the size the fault started with, so the backing's correct "no more bytes" at the new end read as unrecoverable. A writer rewriting a file a reader has already mapped is the ordinary case, and it killed the reader. Fixed by re-reading once, re-deriving the extent per attempt, and failing only on a genuine read error or on a page truncated wholly past the new end (the reference's post-read size re-check, whose answer there is a fault, not a zero page). | `vmm::tests_shortfill::a_read_that_stalls_once_is_re_read_not_made_fatal` and `::a_file_that_shrinks_under_the_fault_is_an_eof_tail_not_a_fatal_short`. Positive control: set `FILL_ATTEMPTS` to 1 and BOTH go red with exactly `Io`, the error that becomes the signal; restored, 395 vmm tests green. The three pre-existing short-fill tests stay green, so the B240 guard against installing a partially-zero page is intact. | Chris Watkins |

Positive control: taking the state from the attr again turns both RED, restored GREEN. | perf lane |
| FIXED F856 | MISSING | HIGH | Row 298: per-task perf event contexts did not exist. A thread's events were a bare list in one table — enough to find them, not enough to say whether two threads carry clones of one context at one version, which is what any mid-life pairing between a parent and a RUNNING child has to decide. `attr.inherit_stat` therefore synchronised only at child exit. `fs::perf::context` now owns each thread's list with a stable identity, a modification generation, the clone lineage stamped at fork (flattened to the root, and only when every event crossed) and the count of events wanting per-task counts; `fs::perf::context::sched_out`, called from the bottom half that already carries a switch's two identities, brings every `inherit_stat` pair up to date and republishes the mapped control page, so a parent's and a running child's own counts are readable mid-life with no syscall at all. | F856. 20 hosted tests in ungated modules (`fs::perf::{context,inherit,registry}`); nine positive controls RED-then-GREEN. | perf lane |

### F1001-native-storage-irq-waits

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED F1001 | DEFECT | HIGH | Native NVMe and AHCI submitted an interrupt-driven request and then unconditionally busy-polled its completion predicate for 200,000 iterations before using the shared wait loop. This burned CPU on each cache-miss I/O and could visibly stall an interactive workload. Linux's normal `nvme_irq` and `ahci_single_level_irq_intr` paths complete IRQ-driven work in their handlers; NVMe polling is reserved for explicitly polled queues. Oxide now enables IRQs for one final predicate recheck and immediately uses the generic publish/recheck/schedule wait contract. | `../linux-master/drivers/nvme/host/pci.c::{nvme_irq,nvme_poll}`; `../linux-master/drivers/ata/libahci.c::ahci_single_level_irq_intr`; `cargo test -p drv-nvme -p drv-ahci --lib -- --test-threads=1` (25 passed). | F1001 |
### F1002-nvme-irq-cq-validation

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED F1002 | DEFECT | HIGH | The NVMe hard IRQ path marked every delivered PCI vector as a completed command. A spurious or stale vector therefore woke the request owner, which found no phase-valid CQE and poisoned a healthy controller. The IRQ endpoint now retains the sole I/O CQ cursor and signals only when its current CQE has the expected phase tag; process context remains the owner that consumes the CQE, rings the CQ doorbell, and republishes the next cursor. | `drv_nvme::regs::tests::cqe_phase_and_cid` pins both matching and mismatching phase predicates; `cargo test -p drv-nvme --lib -- --test-threads=1`. | F1002 |
### F1003-e1000-napi-irq-masking

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED F1003 | DEFECT | HIGH | e1000 acknowledged ICR and scheduled its deferred RX poll while leaving every receive cause enabled. A busy physical NIC could continuously interrupt CPUs while the bounded poll was already responsible for draining the ring, degrading interactive scheduling. The endpoint now owns a NAPI-shaped polling bit: the first valid cause masks the source and schedules NET_RX; the poll keeps it masked while work remains, otherwise checks the latched cause, clears its poll bit, and reenables interrupts so no masked-window event is lost. | `cargo test -p drv-e1000 --lib -- --test-threads=1`; kernel target builds exercise the IRQ-only code path. | F1003 |

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |

| FIXED 0c9c42c4e | COVERAGE | med | `ext4::extent_rw_image::fallocate_sparse_extents_promotes_full_root_to_depth3` was RED on `main`, reddening `cargo test --workspace` for every lane. Not an extent-tree defect: the test constrains external-node `eh_max` to 4 (so the 1 KiB fixture image can exercise a depth-3 tree) by writing the bytes straight to the backing `BlockDevice`, behind `Mount`'s own metadata buffer cache (`crates/kernel/ext4/src/mount/core.rs` `read_metadata_block`). Every insert after the first poke kept reading the pre-poke header out of that cache, so `eh_max` never appeared as 4 to the insertion code and the leaf grew unbounded instead of splitting — root stuck at depth 1 for 90+ inserts, tripping the loop's `< 96` safety assert. ### B2242-bdev-mapping-sleep-under-lock

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED B2242 | DEFECT | high | **The x86 boot's unbounded `scheduling while atomic` storm was a raw block-device read copying page-cache bytes into the caller's USER buffer while holding the block-device mapping spinlock with bottom halves off.** `BdevMapping::read_at`/`write_at` held `st` (rank 40, `Inode` class) across `copy_from_slice` to/from the slice `sys_read`/`sys_write` build straight over the user VA. The first touch of a not-present user page faults, demand paging takes the PMM page lock — a SLEEPING lock — and the scheduler refuses to sleep in an atomic section, so the task spun on the same `[BUG]` record every ~5 ms forever and the boot never reached `getty.target`. The reference does neither thing: its cached read copies out holding only a page REFERENCE (never the page-tree lock, with a voluntary reschedule between pages), and its cached write does the in-place copy with faults DISABLED, retrying after faulting the source in outside the locked section — its own comment names this exact deadlock. Fix: the mapping lock now spans the page copy to/from a staging page and nothing else; the caller's transfer runs through `read_iter`/`write_iter` with no lock held. | B2242. Before (x86 boot log of 2026-08-16 00:29:21, captured in the since-removed `kernel-B2237` worktree): **34,409** identical `held_lock_rank=40 held=[40@crates/kernel/block/src/bdev/mapping.rs:177] caller=.../wait_event.rs:143`, one task (`tid=4199`, constant `sp`), starting 0.1 s after `systemd-zram-setup@zram0.service` began and repeating to the end of the log; that boot never reached `getty.target`. After (`target/boot-logs/after-B2242-x86.log`, kept): **0** `scheduling while atomic` records and 0 `[BUG]` lines; `systemd-zram-setup@zram0.service` FINISHES at 6.018 s, `getty.target` at 4.750 s, `basic.target` at 6.508 s, `boot-smoke: PASS` attempt 1. 4 hosted tests in `block::bdev::tests` (117 passed, was 113); positive control: holding the lock across the caller's transfer turns 3 of the 4 RED, restored GREEN. | B2242-bdev-mapping-sleep-under-lock |

### F1214

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |

| FIXED F1214 | DEFECT | high | **f2fs did not inherit a parent directory's DEFAULT ACL on create/mkdir/mknod.** Every new object took its mode from the umask alone and stored no ACL, so a directory carrying a default ACL granted nothing to the objects created inside it and the mode was whatever the umask left — a permission bug both ways (too open where the ACL narrowed, too closed where it widened). No `posix_acl_create` equivalent existed anywhere in the tree, for any filesystem. | F1214. `mount/ops.rs::make` applied `perm & !ctx.umask` and returned. Now: `vfs::posix_acl::acl_create` + `f2fs::acl::inherit`, reached from `make`; 10 tests in `f2fs/src/tests/acl_ops.rs` drive real inode ops over a real image. Positive control: restoring the umask-only line turns 3 of them RED (the three that assert an inherited mode or record; the three asserting ABSENCE stay green by design). | F1214 |
| FIXED F1214 | DEFECT | high | **f2fs stored the ACL interchange blob verbatim instead of its own on-disk record.** The stored record's header word is 1, not the interchange 2, and its entries are 4 bytes unless they name a user or group; the interchange form is version 2 with a fixed 8 bytes per entry. So every ACL oxide wrote to an f2fs volume was unreadable to Linux (version mismatch → EINVAL) and every ACL Linux wrote was handed to userspace as raw version-1 bytes. | F1214. `mount/ops.rs::{setxattr,getxattr}` passed the value straight through for `system.posix_acl_*`. Now converted at that boundary by `f2fs::acl::{disk_from_xattr,xattr_from_disk}`; `tests/acl.rs` asserts the two forms are different bytes and each conversion inverts the other. Positive control: dropping the conversion turns 5 tests RED. One of them only became able to fail after being strengthened to read the raw stored bytes — before that it compared setxattr against getxattr, which round-trips verbatim with the conversion removed. | F1214 |

| FIXED F1216 | DEFECT | CRITICAL | **An `fsync` over a page rewritten IN PLACE wrote nothing, fenced nothing and returned success, leaving the bytes in the device's volatile cache.** Reachable the moment F1215 (PR #5531) landed in-place update: its mount tuning arms force-IPU on a volume of at most 16x512 main segments, so ordinary writes on small volumes now land back on the block the file's slot ALREADY names and the last checkpoint ALREADY counted. Nothing about the file's recorded shape changes, so `inode_dirty` compares it identical to its checkpointed generation — measured, not inferred: `Dirty { data: false, meta: false }` with an EMPTY device command log out of `sync_file`. `sync_file` then took its "nothing to make durable" early return, so the one thing those bytes needed — a barrier — was the one thing never issued. The reference has a third answer at exactly this point that we had no analogue for: an in-place write sets `FI_UPDATE_WRITE`, and an `fsync` finding it with no out-of-place writes jumps straight to the barrier, writing no recovery chain (there is nothing for one to say about a block the checkpoint already names) and clearing the flag only once the barrier SUCCEEDED. F1216 adds `devices::barrier::{sync_work,UpdateWrites}` (the three-way ladder and the per-inode debt), records the debt at the in-place write site, pays it in `fsync_barrier`, and retires it wholesale at a checkpoint whose commit block actually carried the promise. | F1216, found by the merge of current `main` reddening `a_barrier_flush_is_counted_and_carries_no_bytes` (fs-flush row 0, expected 1). Positive controls, each restored green: deleting the record at the write site reddens 5; making the ladder ignore the debt reddens 3; retiring the debt when no barrier was issued reddens 1; retiring it after a `nobarrier` mount's checkpoint reddens 1. | — |
| FIXED F1216 | DEFECT | CRITICAL | **f2fs made no device-cache barrier of any kind on the `fsync` chain path, and wrote the checkpoint's commit block as an ordinary write.** On a device with a volatile write cache both promises were false: `fsync` returned having written a node chain the drive still held in cache, so a power cut lost acknowledged writes; and the pack's commit block could reach the medium BEFORE the pack it commits, so the next mount could read a whole-looking checkpoint naming blocks that were never written — worse than losing the checkpoint, because nothing detects it. **The filed gap ("no FLUSH-bio / write-barrier command control") was PARTLY STALE:** `commit_body` already called `source.flush_devices()` under `opts.barrier`, so multi-device members were fenced; what was missing was the primary's fence, the fsync barrier, the capability fact, and the ordering. | FIXED F1210 | DEFECT | high | **f2fs compressed files wrote THROUGH, so none of the deferred-allocation path applied to them.** A write to a compressed inode read the cluster back, compressed it and allocated its blocks inside the write call, while every other f2fs data write had moved to write-begin + writeback (PR #5520). ### B2030

### F851

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED F851 | DEFECT | med | virtio-blk's completion poll drained the SAME virtqueue the completion interrupt drives, so a polled ring saved the wait but not the interrupt. Closed by giving the driver a real interrupt-free poll queue: `VIRTIO_BLK_F_MQ` is negotiated, `num_queues` is read from device config, and when the device offers a queue to spare the driver programs a second request queue at the tail of the array with NO MSI-X vector bound and `VRING_AVAIL_F_NO_INTERRUPT` set in its driver area. The whole ring shadow is per-queue (`BlkQueue` owns the resource, the `RingShadow` and the lock), and the two drain contexts now PARTITION the queues: the completion softirq drains only queues whose completions the device signals, a poll drains only the interrupt-free ones. A transfer submitted through the direct path is stamped `polled` and issued on the poll queue; `can_poll` is true only when such a queue exists, so a single-queue device reports no poll capability rather than promising a saving it cannot make. The QEMU launchers pass `num-queues=2` on every virtio-blk device, since one queue is the default and the negotiation would otherwise find nothing to negotiate. | F851. 15 new hosted tests across `drv-virtio-blk` (33→49) and `virtio` (58→61) plus 2 in `block` (85→87): queue-count arithmetic, the tail placement, the never-take-the-last-queue rule, the `avail.flags` suppression store, the softirq/poll partition, the capability gate and the direct path's `polled` stamp. Positive controls, each RED then restored GREEN: cursor not advancing (2 RED), poll queue allowed to take the last default queue (3 RED), suppression store removed (1 RED), `can_poll` hardcoded true (1 RED), softirq draining every queue (1 RED), direct path not stamping `polled` (1 RED), optional queue withheld from the child (1 RED), poll queue given a completion handler (1 RED). ### F859

| Status | Class | Sev | Issue | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIXED F859 | DEFECT | high | **An aarch64 `kexec_file_load(2)` relocation ran and the relocated kernel died in device probe before userspace** — a data abort on a pointer full of `0xc2` bytes inside `__insert_inode_hash` under `bdev_add` under `virtblk_probe`. Cause: this kernel's interrupt controller keeps reading its LPI configuration table and writing its pending table across the jump, and NOTHING told the next kernel. That kernel found LPIs still enabled, adopted the tables the registers pointed at, and rewrote the configuration table over its whole 64 KiB granule — while this kernel had allocated only 16 KiB (one byte per LPI at 14 ID bits), and while the range was in neither the placement map's exclusions nor the handover tree's reservations. The faulting bucket sat at `0xbf33e9a0`, `0x69a0` into the table at `0xbf338000` — past the 16 KiB allocated, inside the 64 KiB rewritten — and `0xc2` is an LPI configuration byte, which is why the value looked like poison and the victim looked unrelated. Fixed on both halves: the tables are allocated at the granule an adopting kernel assumes, and their extents are recorded once and used twice — cut from the placement map so no segment lands there, and carried into the handover tree so the new kernel's allocator never hands them out. NOTE for row below: which CPU runs the relocation decides whether the bug fires at all — the new kernel boots on that CPU's redistributor, and this kernel enables LPIs only on the boot CPU's, so a relocation from a secondary never takes the adopting path. The earlier "the parked secondary is ruled out as the differentiator" reading was wrong. | F859. `scratch/evidence/kexec-arm-file-load-userspace.log`: `kexec -s -l` rc=0, `kexec -e`, second kernel banner from `[0.000000]`, `Run /bin/sh as init process`, shell answers `NEWSH-42`; 2/2 runs reached userspace. The handover reservations are directly measured: the new kernel reports `163408K reserved` against `163280K` before, exactly the two 64 KiB tables. 11 hosted tests (`kexec::file_load::reserved`, `arm_image::handover`, `arm_image::assemble`, `arch_irq::gic_lpi_layout`, `firmware::memreserve`); positive controls — tree reservations dropped -> RED, placement subtraction disabled -> RED (incl. the end-to-end loader test), table sized at `1 << IDbits` -> RED; all restored -> GREEN. | F859 |
